claim: In inattentional blindness (IB), naive observers fail to report clearly visible stimuli when their attention is otherwise engaged.
source: In IB, naive observers fail to report clearly visible stimuli when their attention is otherwise engaged—famously missing a gorilla parading before their eyes.
evidence: This is a well-established finding in the field, supported by citations throughout the manuscript and presented as a foundational premise.

claim: IB carries tremendous significance as evidence that awareness requires attention.
source: IB carries tremendous significance, both as evidence that awareness requires attention and as a tool in seeking the neural correlates of consciousness.
evidence: This represents the orthodox interpretation of IB in the literature, supported by multiple citations.

claim: IB is used as a tool in seeking the neural correlates of consciousness.
source: IB carries tremendous significance, both as evidence that awareness requires attention and as a tool in seeking the neural correlates of consciousness.
evidence: This is supported by citations to neuroscience studies using IB paradigms.

claim: The implications of IB rest on a notoriously biased measure: asking participants whether they noticed anything unusual.
source: However, such implications rest on a notoriously biased measure: asking participants whether they noticed anything unusual (and interpreting negative answers as reflecting a complete lack of perception).
evidence: This is a critical methodological claim supported by signal detection theory principles and cited literature on response bias.

claim: Inattentionally blind participants can successfully report the location, color, and shape of stimuli they deny noticing.
source: Here, in the largest ever set of IB studies, we show that, as a group, inattentionally blind participants can successfully report the location, color, and shape of stimuli they deny noticing, demonstrating that perceptual information remains accessible in IB.
evidence: This is the primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data from five experiments.

claim: Observers are collectively biased to report not noticing in IB.
source: By introducing absent trials, we further show that observers are collectively biased to report not noticing in IB—essentially 'playing it safe' in reporting their sensitivity.
evidence: This is supported by signal detection theory analysis of absent trials in the experiments.

claim: The data provide the strongest evidence to date of significant residual visual sensitivity in IB.
source: These data provide the strongest evidence to date of significant residual visual sensitivity in IB.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on the experimental findings and comparison to prior literature.

claim: The findings challenge the use of inattentional blindness to argue that awareness requires attention.
source: They also challenge the use of inattentional blindness to argue that awareness requires attention.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental findings showing residual sensitivity.

claim: IB is perhaps the best-known result in contemporary perception science.
source: However, this seemingly secure assumption is challenged by perhaps the best-known result in contemporary perception science: The phenomenon of inattentional blindness (IB).
evidence: This is a characterization of the field's reception of IB, supported by its widespread citation and public recognition.

claim: IB is an extremely robust phenomenon, demonstrated in a stunning variety of laboratory and real-world contexts across half a century of research.
source: IB is an extremely robust phenomenon, demonstrated in a stunning variety of laboratory and real-world contexts across half a century of research (Neisser and Becklen, 1975; Moore and Egeth, 1997; Mack and Rock, 1998; Simons and Chabris, 1999; Most et al., 2005; Drew et al., 2013; Murphy and Greene, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by extensive citations to the IB literature spanning decades.

claim: The IB rate can be remarkably high, over 80% in some of Mack & Rock's studies.
source: Although the proportion of subjects demonstrating IB (the 'IB rate') varies widely depending on the protocol, it can be remarkably high (e.g. ~50% in the case of the famous gorilla, and over 80% in some of Mack & Rock's studies; for reviews see Simons, 2000; De Brigard and Prinz, 2010; Jensen et al., 2011; de P Nobre et al., 2020; Redlich et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to specific studies and review articles.

claim: According to the 'consensus view', subjects undergoing IB 'have no awareness at all of the stimulus object'.
source: According to the 'consensus view' (Noah and Mangun, 2020; see also Mack and Rock, 1998; Dehaene et al., 2006; Cohen et al., 2012; Prinz, 2012; Prinz, 2015; though see Koch and Tsuchiya, 2007; Maier and Tsuchiya, 2021), subjects undergoing IB 'have no awareness at all of the stimulus object' (Rock et al., 1992), such that 'one can have one's eyes focused on an object or event … without seeing it at all' (Carruthers, 2015).
evidence: This is the orthodox interpretation of IB, supported by multiple citations to the literature.

claim: IB is a key piece of evidence for the claim that awareness requires attention.
source: First, IB is a key piece of evidence for the more general claim that awareness requires attention (or, conversely, that 'without attention, conscious perception cannot occur'; Dehaene et al., 2006), and so has been used to support various leading theories of consciousness on which attention plays a critical role, such as global neuronal workspace theory (Dehaene and Naccache, 2001), attended intermediate representation (AIR) theory (Prinz, 2015), and attention schema theory (Graziano and Webb, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to theories of consciousness that rely on IB evidence.

claim: IB is frequently used by neuroscientists to measure neural activity in the absence of consciousness.
source: Second, conceived as a tool to abolish awareness, IB is frequently used by neuroscientists to measure neural activity in the absence of consciousness (e.g. Rees et al., 1999; Pitts et al., 2014; Hutchinson, 2019), in the hope of isolating the neural correlates of consciousness.
evidence: This is supported by citations to neuroscience studies using IB paradigms.

claim: Yes/no questions are inherently and notoriously subject to bias.
source: However, yes/no questions of this sort are inherently and notoriously subject to bias, because they require observers to set a criterion in order to decide whether they have enough evidence to answer 'yes' or instead answer 'no' (Dulany, 2001; cf. Eriksen, 1960; Holender, 1986; Irvine, 2012).
evidence: This is a principle from signal detection theory and psychophysics, supported by citations.

claim: Under Signal Detection Theory, observers must set a criterion to determine whether a signal is present.
source: Under the framework of Signal Detection Theory (SDT; Tanner and Swets, 1954; Green and Swets, 1966), observers who are asked to determine whether a signal is or is not present must in setting such a criterion consider tradeoffs between the various possible outcomes of their decision (i.e. the relative costs of hits, misses, false alarms, and correct rejections).
evidence: This is a foundational principle of signal detection theory, supported by citations to classic SDT texts.

claim: Observers in IB tasks may have reason to be conservative in their criterion-setting.
source: Indeed, in an IB task (where the signal in question is the unexpected stimulus), observers may have reason to be conservative in their criterion-setting—that is to adopt a high standard for saying 'yes' (and answer 'no' if that standard isn't met).
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction based on SDT principles applied to IB tasks.

claim: Subjects might respond 'no' out of an excess of caution due to under-confidence.
source: For example, observers might be under-confident whether they saw anything (or whether what they saw counted as unusual); this might lead them to respond 'no' out of an excess of caution.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for conservative responding in IB tasks.

claim: Subjects may worry that reporting noticing the unexpected object will suggest they weren't engaged in the primary task.
source: Subjects may also worry that if they report noticing the unexpected object, the experimenters will take that to mean they weren't engaged in the task they had been given (e.g. judging which cross arm was longer or counting the passes; Dulany, 2001).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for conservative responding, supported by a citation.

claim: Evidence for conservative reporting would have dramatic consequences for the dominant interpretation of IB.
source: Evidence for this alternative hypothesis would have dramatic consequences for the dominant interpretation of IB and the implications that follow from it: It would overturn the view that IB reflects a total failure to perceive and so challenge the appeal to IB in arguments that attention is required for awareness.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the implications of the study's hypothesis.

claim: The hypothesis that subjects in IB see more than they say remains empirically unsettled.
source: Remarkably, however, the hypothesis that subjects in inattentional blindness tasks actually see more than they say (but respond otherwise because they are conservative in reporting their awareness) remains empirically unsettled, and the powerful tools of SDT unexploited in relation to IB.
evidence: This is a characterization of the state of the literature prior to the current study.

claim: A recent meta-analysis argues that prior work on residual sensitivity in IB is problematic due to underpowered samples and publication bias.
source: However, a recent meta-analysis of this literature (de P Nobre et al., 2022) argues that such work is problematic along a number of dimensions, including underpowered samples and evidence of publication bias that, when corrected for, eliminates effects revealed by earlier approaches, concluding 'that more evidence, particularly from well-powered pre-registered experiments, is needed before solid conclusions can be drawn regarding implicit processing during inattentional blindness' (de P Nobre et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a summary of findings from a cited meta-analysis.

claim: The study ran 25,000 subjects, each experiencing just a single critical trial.
source: Third, we leverage online data collection to massively increase sample size (running 25,000 subjects, each experiencing just a single critical trial), in order to make possible the crucial signal-detection analyses that separate bias from sensitivity.
evidence: This is a description of the study's methodology.

claim: The study introduces a novel analytic approach by applying signal detection models to a 'super subject'.
source: Finally, to overcome the fact that in IB each subject necessarily only contributes one trial (since following a critical trial, stimuli are no longer unexpected), we introduce a novel analytic approach by applying signal detection models to a 'super subject'.
evidence: This is a description of the study's novel methodological contribution.

claim: In Experiment 1, 28.6% of subjects responded 'no' they didn't notice anything unusual.
source: In line with established findings on IB, a considerable proportion of subjects (28.6%) responded 'no' they didn't notice anything unusual (we refer to these subjects across all our experiments as 'non-noticers').
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental data, also shown in Figure 2b.

claim: In Experiment 1, 63.6% of non-noticers answered the forced-choice location question correctly.
source: This is precisely what we found: 63.6% of non-noticers answered the forced-choice question correctly (significantly different from the 50% correct expected by chance in a two-sided binomial probability test, 95% CI = [0.54, 0.73], BF10 = 9.9).
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental data with statistical analysis, also shown in Figure 2c.

claim: In Experiment 1, non-noticers' sensitivity to location was d′2afc = 0.51, 95% CI = [0.16, 0.85].
source: Critically, this result also holds using d′, an unbiased measure of sensitivity (d′2afc = 0.51, 95% CI = [0.16, 0.85]; see Box 1 on SDT), which we use in reporting all following results concerning sensitivity in non-noticers.
evidence: This is a direct report of signal detection analysis of experimental data, also shown in Figure 2c.

claim: In Experiment 2, only 72.3% of subjects shown an additional stimulus said they had noticed something.
source: This experiment yielded similar results to Experiment 1: Only 72.3% of subjects shown an additional stimulus said they had noticed something, yet 81% were able to indicate the additional line's color correctly.
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental data.

claim: In Experiment 2, non-noticers demonstrated above chance sensitivity to color (d′ = 0.38, 95% CI = [0.03, 0.73]).
source: And again, as a group, non-noticers demonstrated above chance sensitivity, this time to color (d′ = 0.38, 95% CI = [0.03, 0.73]).
evidence: This is a direct report of signal detection analysis of experimental data, also shown in Figure 3b.

claim: In Experiment 2, subjects displayed a significant bias in favor of responding 'blue' (c = 0.67, 95% CI = [0.49, 0.84]).
source: Note that the unbiased nature of this measure is especially critical here since subjects displayed a significant bias in favor of responding 'blue' (c = 0.67, 95% CI = [0.49, 0.84]).
evidence: This is a direct report of signal detection analysis of experimental data.

claim: In Experiment 2, subjects were conservative in reporting their awareness (c = 0.31, 95% CI = [0.22, 0.41]).
source: This analysis revealed evidence for the second aspect of our alternative hypothesis: Not only do subjects collectively have residual sensitivity to unnoticed IB stimuli, they are, as a group, conservative in reporting their awareness (c = 0.31, 95% CI = [0.22, 0.41]; d′ = 1.81, 95% CI = [1.63, 1.99]; note that statistics here are for all subjects).
evidence: This is a direct report of signal detection analysis of experimental data, also shown in Figure 5c.

claim: In Experiment 3, high-confidence non-noticers collectively demonstrated significantly above-chance sensitivity to location (d′2afc = 0.34; 95% CI = [0.08, 0.60]).
source: Remarkably, even this group of subjects (N=204) collectively demonstrated significantly above-chance sensitivity to the location of the IB stimulus (d′2afc = 0.34; 95% CI = [0.08, 0.60]).
evidence: This is a direct report of signal detection analysis of experimental data, also shown in Figure 3e.

claim: In Experiment 3, subjects' confidence in their yes/no response predicted accuracy on the discrimination task.
source: Further, as is evident from Figure 3e, subjects' confidence in their yes/no response predicted accuracy for that group on the discrimination task, suggesting that subjects may have graded awareness of unattended stimuli in IB tasks (see Appendix for details).
evidence: This is an inference from the pattern of data shown in Figure 3e.

claim: In Experiment 4, 57.3% of subjects demonstrated IB.
source: Consistent with previous studies using dynamic stimuli (see Figure 1b and c), a majority of subjects—57.3%—demonstrated IB.
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental data.

claim: In Experiment 4, non-noticers collectively demonstrated significant sensitivity to color (d′ = 0.82, 95% CI = [0.61, 1.04]) and shape (d′ = 0.21, 95% CI = [0.01, 0.42]).
source: However, despite the attentionally demanding primary task, non-noticers collectively again demonstrated significant sensitivity to the features of the IB stimulus, choosing the correct color (d′ = 0.82, 95% CI = [0.61, 1.04]) and shape (d′ = 0.21, 95% CI = [0.01, 0.42]) significantly more often than would be predicted by chance.
evidence: This is a direct report of signal detection analysis of experimental data.

claim: In Experiment 4, subjects underreported their awareness with a conservative criterion (c = 0.85, 95% CI = [0.73, 0.97]).
source: Just as in Experiment 2, subjects underreported their awareness of the IB stimulus on the traditional yes/no question, employing a decision criterion that was even more conservative than that measured in Experiment 2 (c = 0.85, 95% CI = [0.73, 0.97]; d′ = 1.33, 95% CI = [1.10, 1.57]; again, note that statistics here are for all subjects; see Figure 5c).
evidence: This is a direct report of signal detection analysis of experimental data, also shown in Figure 5c.

claim: In Experiment 4, the IB rate for color-incongruent stimuli was substantially higher than for color-congruent stimuli (86.57% vs 28.71%).
source: Specifically, the IB rate for color-incongruent stimuli was substantially higher than for color-congruent stimuli (86.57% vs 28.71%), suggesting suppression occurred.
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental data showing a color congruency effect.

claim: In Experiment 5, non-noticers collectively performed above-chance in discriminating both color (d′ = 0.12, 95% CI = [0.02, 0.23]) and shape (d′ = 0.23, 95% CI = [0.13, 0.33]).
source: Remarkably, even under these conditions (and with the concern about color congruency effects mitigated), the pattern of results matched that of Experiment 4: Subjects collectively performed above-chance in discriminations of both color (d′ = 0.12, 95% CI = [0.02, 0.23]) and shape (d′ = 0.23, 95% CI = [0.13, 0.33]), but not location (d′2afc = 0.03, 95% CI = [–0.04, 0.11]) (see Figure 4b).
evidence: This is a direct report of signal detection analysis of experimental data, also shown in Figure 4b.

claim: In Experiment 5, subjects were collectively biased to respond 'no' to the traditional yes/no IB question (c = 0.45, 95% CI = [0.41, 0.49]).
source: Further, we again found that subjects were collectively biased to respond 'no' to the traditional yes/no IB question (c = 0.45, 95% CI = [0.41, 0.49]; d′ = 2.01, 95% CI = [1.94, 2.09]; statistics here are for all subjects; see Figure 5c).
evidence: This is a direct report of signal detection analysis of experimental data, also shown in Figure 5c.

claim: Experiment 5 was the largest single inattentional blindness sample ever collected.
source: After exclusions, 10,830 subjects in total, including 2339 non-noticers, were included in the analysis. (To our knowledge, this made Experiment 5 the largest single inattentional blindness sample ever collected.)
evidence: This is a characterization of the study's sample size relative to the literature.

claim: The experiments employed designs and protocols closely modeled on canonical IB studies.
source: Our experiments all employed designs and protocols closely modeled on canonical IB studies. In Experiments 1–3, we studied IB using a cross task closely modeled on Mack and Rock's classic studies (Mack and Rock, 1998). In Experiments 4–5, we studied IB using a dynamic task closely modeled on Wood and Simons, 2017 (itself adapted from influential work by Most et al., 2001; Most et al., 2005; Ward and Scholl, 2015).
evidence: This is a description of the study's methodological approach, supported by citations.

claim: The study eschewed the use of divided and full attention trials.
source: Our approach also eschews the use of divided and full attention trials.
evidence: This is a description of a methodological choice in the study design.

claim: The use of divided and full attention trial exclusions has been argued to 'lead researchers to understate the pervasiveness of inattentional blindness'.
source: However, this practice is controversial and has been argued to 'lead researchers to understate the pervasiveness of inattentional blindness' (White et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a citation to a methodological critique in the literature.

claim: The study adopted a novel analytical approach, applying signal detection models to a 'super subject'.
source: To assess objective sensitivity and bias in IB, we adopted a novel analytical approach, applying signal detection models to a 'super subject' whose responses are comprised of individual subjects' responses in their single critical trials.
evidence: This is a description of the study's analytical methodology.

claim: Violation of the equal variance assumption in SDT could lead to under- or over-estimation of d′ and c, but any such estimation would be slight.
source: However, empirically, equal variance might not hold in one-interval tasks. Violation of this equal variance assumption could lead to under- or over-estimation of d′ and c. However, any such under- or over-estimation would be slight and unlikely to affect our main results.
evidence: This is a methodological consideration with supporting calculations provided in the text.

claim: Many follow-up questions in prior IB studies are used to include subjects in the IB group rather than exclude them.
source: First, follow-up questions are often used not to exclude subjects from the IB group but to include subjects. For example, Most et al., 2001 treated as inattentionally blind not only subjects who denied noticing the unexpected object but also subjects who claimed they did notice the object but were subsequently unable to describe it.
evidence: This is a critique of prior methodological practices, supported by citations.

claim: Most follow-up questions in prior IB studies remain subject to response bias in the same way as the original yes/no awareness question.
source: Second, most follow-up questions remain subject to response bias in just the same way as the original yes/no awareness question.
evidence: This is a methodological critique based on signal detection theory principles.

claim: Many follow-up questions in prior IB studies are insufficiently sensitive, especially with small sample sizes.
source: Third, and finally, many follow-up questions are insufficiently sensitive (especially with small sample sizes).
evidence: This is a methodological critique with examples from the literature.

claim: A recent meta-analysis concluded that more evidence from well-powered pre-registered experiments is needed regarding implicit processing during inattentional blindness.
source: The authors of this meta-analysis conclude with the following recommendation for future work: 'We suggest that more evidence, particularly from well-powered pre-registered experiments, is needed before solid conclusions can be drawn regarding implicit processing during inattentional blindness' (de P Nobre et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a direct quote from a cited meta-analysis.

claim: The present set of studies provides the evidence recommended by the meta-analysis.
source: We see the present set of high-powered pre-registered studies as providing precisely this evidence, in ways that advance our understanding of IB considerably.
evidence: This is a claim about the contribution of the current study, based on its design and findings.

claim: Unexpected line patterns have been found to elicit the same Nd1 ERP component in both noticers and inattentionally blind subjects.
source: For example, in the electrophysiology literature, unexpected line patterns have been found to elicit the same Nd1 ERP component in both noticers and inattentionally blind subjects (Pitts et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a citation to prior electrophysiology research on IB.

claim: Preserved neural signatures of scene segmentation and perceptual inference have been found in inattentionally blind subjects.
source: Likewise, preserved neural signatures of scene segmentation and perceptual inference (e.g. Kanizsa figures) have been found in inattentionally blind subjects (see respectively, Scholte et al., 2006; Vandenbroucke et al., 2014), although interestingly not differential responses to meaningful words versus meaningless letter strings (Rees et al., 1999).
evidence: This is a citation to prior neuroscience research on IB.

claim: Behavioral studies show that unattended stimuli can influence the accuracy and speed of inattentionally blind subjects' judgments in a primary task.
source: Similarly, behavioral studies show that unattended stimuli can influence the accuracy and speed of inattentionally blind subjects' judgments in a primary task (e.g. Moore and Egeth, 1997; replicated in Wood and Simons, 2019; Pugnaghi et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a citation to prior behavioral research on IB.

claim: The results raise an alternative explanation that inattentionally blind subjects may retain a degree of awareness of IB stimuli.
source: Although some researchers have interpreted these results as implying a kind of subliminal processing of IB stimuli, our results just as easily raise an alternative (and perhaps more straightforward) explanation: that inattentionally blind subjects may retain a degree of awareness of these stimuli after all.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the current study's findings in relation to prior research.

claim: Above-chance performance in the experiments could be taken to reflect unconscious representations akin to orthodox interpretations of blindsight.
source: We acknowledge that above-chance performance in our experiments could be taken to reflect unconscious representations in a manner akin to orthodox interpretations of blindsight (Weiskrantz et al., 1974; Kolb and Braun, 1995; although see Phillips, 2021b; Morgan et al., 1997; and, for more general skepticism, Newell and Shanks, 2023).
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of an alternative interpretation, with citations.

claim: Explicit voluntary judgments of stimulus features constitute prima facie evidence of conscious processing.
source: However, in our view, explicit voluntary judgments of stimulus features (especially in neurotypical subjects) constitute prima facie evidence of conscious processing, and should be interpreted that way unless there is some compelling reason to favor an alternative (Snodgrass, 2002; Balsdon and Azzopardi, 2015; Heeks and Azzopardi, 2015; Phillips, 2021a).
evidence: This is a theoretical position supported by citations to the consciousness literature.

claim: The results are consistent with some degree of inattentional amnesia.
source: Our results are consistent with some degree of inattentional amnesia, and likewise, with what Block, 2001 calls inattentional inaccessibility.
evidence: This is an inference about the compatibility of the findings with alternative theoretical accounts.

claim: The findings suggest that inattentional amnesia cannot be the whole story, since some features of unexpected objects are available for later explicit report.
source: However, our findings suggest that inattentional amnesia cannot be the whole story, since they reveal that some features of unexpected objects are available for later explicit report even in the group of subjects who deny noticing anything unusual.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: The findings lend support to a more graded perspective on IB and visual awareness.
source: A further upshot of our findings is that they lend support to a more graded perspective on IB (in particular) and both perception and visual awareness (in general).
evidence: This is an inference about the theoretical implications of the findings.

claim: The data suggest that inattention degrades but does not eliminate perception and awareness.
source: Our data suggest the need to move beyond such binaries (cf. Cohen et al., 2023): Inattention degrades but does not eliminate perception and awareness – and likewise explicit encoding.
evidence: This is an inference about the nature of inattention's effects, based on the experimental findings.

claim: The results provide the strongest evidence so far of significant residual visual sensitivity across a range of visual features in IB.
source: Taken together, and after decades of inconclusive findings, the results of our five studies offer the strongest evidence so far of significant residual visual sensitivity across a range of visual features in IB.
evidence: This is a summary claim about the study's contribution, based on the experimental findings.

claim: The results call into question the orthodox interpretation of IB on which inattention entirely abolishes awareness.
source: Together with our finding that subjects collectively exhibit a systematically conservative bias in reporting their awareness, our results also call into question the orthodox interpretation of IB on which inattention entirely abolishes awareness, suggesting that a reconceptualization of inattentional blindness may be required.
evidence: This is an inference about the theoretical implications of the findings.

claim: Inattentional blindness provides evidence that awareness of certain features survives inattention.
source: Indeed, perhaps ironically, inattentional blindness if anything provides evidence that awareness of certain features survives inattention.
evidence: This is an inference about the implications of the findings for understanding IB.

claim: The results highlight the critical value of assessing response bias and including objective measures of sensitivity in studying inattentional blindness and visual awareness.
source: Our results highlight the critical value of assessing response bias and including objective measures of sensitivity in studying inattentional blindness and visual awareness.
evidence: This is a methodological conclusion drawn from the study's approach and findings.

claim: The results point to a broader rethinking of perception and consciousness as graded, rather than binary, phenomena.
source: They also point to a broader rethinking of perception and consciousness as graded, rather than binary, phenomena.
evidence: This is a theoretical implication drawn from the findings.

claim: All sample sizes, exclusion criteria, analyses, and key experimental parameters were pre-registered.
source: All sample sizes, exclusion criteria, analyses, and key experimental parameters reported here have been pre-registered.
evidence: This is a statement about the study's methodological rigor.

claim: Data, analyses, stimuli, and pre-registrations are publicly available at https://osf.io/fcrhu/.
source: Data, analyses, stimuli, and pre-registrations are publicly available at https://osf.io/fcrhu/.
evidence: This is a statement about data availability.

claim: In Experiment 1, 500 adults were recruited from Prolific.
source: 500 adults were recruited from the online platform Prolific (for validation of the reliability of this subject pool, see Peer et al., 2017), with participation limited to US subjects.
evidence: This is a description of the participant recruitment for Experiment 1.

claim: In Experiment 1, after exclusions, 374 subjects were included in the analysis.
source: After excluding subjects who incorrectly reported which arm of the cross was longer on any of Trials 1–3 and those who failed to provide a complete dataset, or failed a test for color vision (Ishihara color plate; see data archive), 374 subjects were included in the analysis.
evidence: This is a description of the final sample size after exclusions for Experiment 1.

claim: The study was approved by the Homewood Institutional Review Board of Johns Hopkins University (protocol number: HIRB00005762).
source: This experiment and all others reported here were approved by the Homewood Institutional Review Board of Johns Hopkins University (protocol number: HIRB00005762).
evidence: This is a statement about ethical approval.

claim: All subjects provided informed consent and were compensated financially for their participation.
source: All subjects provided informed consent and were compensated financially for their participation.
evidence: This is a statement about ethical procedures.

claim: In Experiment 1, on Trials 1-3, a cross appeared for 200 ms either 150 px above or below the fixation circle.
source: The keypress was followed by a 1500 ms delay, after which a cross formed by two thin black lines (3 px thickness; 200 px x 140 px dimensions) appeared for 200 ms either 150 px above or below the fixation circle.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental stimuli and procedure, also illustrated in Figure 2a.

claim: In Experiment 1, on the fourth critical trial, a vertical red line appeared on one side of the display simultaneous with the cross.
source: The fourth, critical trial proceeded the same way, except that simultaneous with the cross, a vertical red line (200 px long; 3 px thick; RGB(147,0,0)) appeared on one side of the display (10 px from the boundary of the display), also for 200 ms.
evidence: This is a description of the critical trial procedure, also illustrated in Figure 2a.

claim: In Experiment 2, 1700 adults were recruited from Prolific.
source: 1700 adults were recruited from Prolific, collected in batches of 100 subjects until a target number of 100 non-noticers was reached.
evidence: This is a description of participant recruitment for Experiment 2.

claim: In Experiment 2, after exclusions, 1261 subjects were included in the analysis.
source: After excluding subjects who incorrectly reported which arm of the cross was longer on any of Trials 1–3 and those who failed to provide a complete dataset, or failed a test for color vision, 1261 subjects were included in the analysis.
evidence: This is a description of the final sample size after exclusions for Experiment 2.

claim: In Experiment 2, the extra vertical line could be either red or blue.
source: The fourth, critical trial proceeded the same way as Experiment 1, except that the extra vertical line that appeared simultaneous with the cross was either red (RGB(147,0,0)) or blue (RGB(0,0,136)), with the color and location of the line randomized across subjects.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental manipulation in Experiment 2, also illustrated in Figure 3a.

claim: In Experiment 3, 7000 subjects were recruited from Prolific.
source: 7000 subjects were recruited from Prolific, and data were collected in batches until we reached 200 non-noticers who reported being 'highly confident' in their yes/no response.
evidence: This is a description of participant recruitment for Experiment 3.

claim: In Experiment 3, after exclusions, 5296 subjects were included in the analysis.
source: After excluding duplicate data files, subjects who incorrectly reported which arm of the cross was longer on any of Trials 1–3, those who failed to provide a complete dataset, or failed a test for color vision, 5296 subjects were included in the analysis.
evidence: This is a description of the final sample size after exclusions for Experiment 3.

claim: In Experiment 4, 1500 subjects were recruited from Prolific.
source: 1500 subjects were recruited from Prolific, and data were collected in batches until we reached 100 non-noticers who answered the color discrimination question first, 100 non-noticers who answered the shape discrimination question first, and 100 non-noticers who answered the location discrimination question first (more on these three discrimination questions below).
evidence: This is a description of participant recruitment for Experiment 4.

claim: In Experiment 4, after exclusions, 1278 subjects including 417 non-noticers remained in the analysis.
source: After exclusions, 1278 subjects including 417 non-noticers remained in the analysis for Experiment 4.
evidence: This is a description of the final sample size after exclusions for Experiment 4.

claim: In Experiment 4, subjects participated in a sustained inattentional blindness task modified from Wood and Simons, 2017.
source: In Experiment 4, subjects participated in a sustained inattentional blindness task modified slightly from experimental code published by Wood and Simons, 2017.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental paradigm used in Experiment 4.

claim: In Experiment 4, subjects' task was to count the number of times squares of a particular color bounced off the perimeter of a gray rectangle.
source: All subjects completed three trials of a dynamic, multiple object tracking task containing black squares and white squares. At the beginning of the experiment, each subject was told whether they should attend to the black or white squares. At the beginning of each trial, subjects were instructed to fixate on a small blue square (11 px x 11 px; RGB(0,0,255)) in the center of a gray (RGB(127,127,127)) rectangle (666 px x 546 px), and were told that their task was to count the number of times the squares of their attended color bounced off of the walls of the gray rectangle.
evidence: This is a description of the primary task in Experiment 4, also illustrated in Figure 4a.

claim: In Experiment 4, on the critical trial, 3/4 of subjects were shown an unexpected shape that remained on screen for 5 s.
source: The critical trial was Trial 3. In this trial, 3/4 of subjects (Present condition) were shown an unexpected shape (a circle or a triangle, which was either black or white). This unexpected object entered the display on either the left or the right 5 s after the trial began, and moved either upward or downward until it exited the other side of the display (thus, there were 2 color x 2 shape x 2 side x 2 motion direction options for IB stimuli, randomly chosen for each subject).
evidence: This is a description of the critical trial procedure in Experiment 4, also illustrated in Figure 4a.

claim: In Experiment 5, subjects were recruited from the USA, Canada, the United Kingdom, and Australia.

evidence: This is a description of participant recruitment for Experiment 5.

claim: In Experiment 5, data were collected until at least 2200 non-noticers were reached.
source: In order to reduce the size of the confidence intervals around the sensitivity estimates relative to Experiment 4, we collected data until we reached at least 2200 subjects who reported not noticing the unexpected stimulus.
evidence: This is a description of the sampling strategy for Experiment 5.

claim: In Experiment 5, every subject was assigned to attend to the white squares in the primary task.
source: Experiment 5 repeated the design of Experiment 4, with two key differences: (1) Every subject was assigned to attend to the white squares in the primary task, (2) the IB stimuli were either orange or green—two colors that as a pair produced equal IB rates in pilot testing.
evidence: This is a description of a key methodological change in Experiment 5.

claim: In Experiment 5, the IB stimuli were either orange or green.
source: Experiment 5 repeated the design of Experiment 4, with two key differences: (1) Every subject was assigned to attend to the white squares in the primary task, (2) the IB stimuli were either orange or green—two colors that as a pair produced equal IB rates in pilot testing.
evidence: This is a description of the stimulus colors used in Experiment 5.

claim: In Experiment 5, for subjects shown no unexpected stimulus, 52.95% guessed orange and 47.05% guessed green.
source: For subjects shown no unexpected stimulus on the critical trial (the Absent condition), 52.95% guessed that the extra object had been orange, and 47.05% guessed that it had been green.
evidence: This is a report of response bias data from Experiment 5.

claim: The log-linear correction adds 0.5 to all cells of the decision matrix to prevent infinite d′.
source: SDT analyses began by calculating the number of hits, false alarms, present trials, and absent trials, and then applying the log-linear correction of adding 0.5 to all cells of the decision matrix (Hautus, 1995; see also Box 1). This is a standard correction to prevent an infinite d′ in the event that either hits or false alarms are zero (this correction was applied to all experiments, although neither hits nor false alarms were ever zero), and simulations have shown that if anything, this correction underestimates d′ (Hautus, 1995).
evidence: This is a description of a standard SDT correction procedure, supported by citations.

claim: Standard error for SDT calculations was estimated using methods described by Macmillan and Creelman, 2005.
source: Because each subject in the experiment contributes just one trial, the signal detection metrics were calculated at the group level, and the standard error for each SDT calculation was estimated using methods described by Macmillan and Creelman, 2005, pgs. 325–328; see also Kadlec, 1999.
evidence: This is a description of the statistical methods used, supported by citations.
